chapters.title: Chapter 1: The Unlisted Market — What It Is and How It Works

lessons.title: Why Indian Unicorns Are Staying Private for Longer

children.text: A week after passing on the WhatsApp broker's Vayu Mobility pitch, Meena runs into an old colleague who works in venture capital. She asks him a simple question: if Vayu Mobility is genuinely a strong company, why has it stayed unlisted for eight years already, and why might it take years more? His answer surprises her. Twenty years ago, a company at Vayu Mobility's size would almost certainly already be listed. Today, staying private for a decade or longer is normal, even for well-run companies.

body.text: An unlisted company today can raise more money, for longer, without ever touching a public market, than an unlisted company could twenty years ago. That is the single biggest reason "pre-IPO" timelines run much longer than most buyers expect.

children.text: The Old Rule: Public Markets Used to Fund Growth

For much of India's post-liberalisation history, an IPO was less a choice and more a necessity. Once a private company outgrew what its promoters, banks and a handful of domestic mutual funds and private equity investors could fund, a public listing was often the only realistic way to raise meaningful growth capital. That meant companies listed comparatively early, sometimes within five to seven years of a serious scale-up phase, well before they reached the size or track record that today's largest unlisted companies already carry.
What Changed: A Flood of Late-Stage Private Capital

markDefs.definition: Large private funding rounds, typically Series C onward, provided by growth-equity funds, sovereign wealth funds and large venture funds, that let a company raise significant capital without listing on a stock exchange.

A state-owned investment fund, such as Singapore's GIC and Temasek or the UAE's ADIA and Mubadala, that invests a government's reserves, including into late-stage private rounds of companies like Indian startups.

children.text: Over the last decade and a half, a very different pool of capital opened up. Global growth-equity funds, dedicated venture funds focused specifically on

began writing large cheques directly into Indian companies, specifically so those companies would not need to list to keep growing. A company can now raise a round worth several thousand crore rupees at a multi-billion-dollar valuation and never touch a stock exchange in the process.

children.text: Why Founders Actually Prefer to Wait

More private capital only explains why staying unlisted became possible. It does not explain why founders actively choose it. A listed company must comply with SEBI's quarterly disclosure obligations and answer to public shareholders whose sentiment can swing the stock daily on news that has little to do with the underlying business. Staying private lets a founder fix weak unit economics, restructure the cap table, or absorb a rough quarter without that being priced into a public stock in real time. It also means early investors and employees can often get liquidity through a private secondary sale, which used to be one of the strongest reasons to rush toward an IPO in the first place.

body.text: Staying private for a decade or longer is not automatically a red flag. Several genuinely strong Indian companies have made this choice deliberately, for sound business reasons. What it does mean, without exception, is that an investor buying that company's unlisted shares should expect their capital to stay locked up for a long and genuinely uncertain period, not a quick one.

body.title: Staying Private Longer: Questions to Ask Before You Read Too Much Into It
steps: How many funding rounds has the company raised since its last known valuation, and who led them?
Has any existing investor publicly or reportedly marked down the company's valuation?
Is there a specific IPO timeline backed by a filed DRHP, or just a general "IPO is coming" expectation?
How does the company's growth and profitability compare with peers that have already listed?
What is the realistic worst case if the IPO is delayed by another three to five years?

children.text: When the Wait Doesn't End the Way Investors Expect

body.label: Not every "pre-IPO" story ends in an IPO
body.value: Staying private longer is not risk-free
body.context: Some heavily funded Indian startups have seen their own investors mark down their valuations sharply, with a long-anticipated public listing never materialising.

children.text: Two very different real examples show the range of outcomes. Byju's, once counted among India's most valuable startups, saw several of its own investors mark down their holdings sharply within a couple of years, and its long-discussed IPO never happened. Paytm, on the other hand, did list, several years after its last major private funding round, but its shares fell well below the IPO price within months of listing, eroding a large part of the paper gains that late-stage private investors had been counting on. Staying private longer changes when and whether an exit happens. It does not, by itself, change whether that exit is a profitable one.

body.text: An eventual IPO is not automatically a profitable exit. If you buy unlisted shares based on a private funding round's valuation, your actual return depends on where the public market prices the company on listing day and afterward, not on the valuation you paid to get in.

body.title: A 20% Discount to an Old Number
body.scenario: A different dealer offers Meena shares in a logistics startup that last raised private funding four years ago at a ₹4,000 crore valuation. He says the company is "IPO-bound next year" and is pricing the shares at a 20% discount to that four-year-old valuation.
body.prompt: What should Meena think about before treating that 20% discount as a bargain?
body.modelAnswer: A valuation set four years ago is stale by default. In that time the company could have grown well past it, stagnated, or been quietly marked down by its own investors, and a 20% discount to an unverified, years-old number says nothing about whether today's fair value is higher or lower than that. "IPO-bound next year" needs the same check as any pre-IPO claim: is there a DRHP filed with SEBI, or just the dealer's word? And even if the company does list on schedule, Meena has already seen that listing-day and post-listing pricing can fall well below the last private valuation. A discount on a number that was never verified in the first place is not automatically cheap.

body.title: Reading "Staying Private Longer" Correctly
body.question: Which statement best describes what it means for a buyer of unlisted shares when a company has stayed unlisted for 10+ years?
options: It guarantees the company is high quality, since only strong companies can avoid an IPO for that long
It has no bearing on investment risk, since ownership rights are identical whether a company is listed or not
It means the buyer's capital could stay illiquid for a long, uncertain period, with no guarantee the eventual outcome preserves the price paid
It means the company automatically gets listed once it turns profitable, since profitability is the only real listing requirement
body.explanation: Staying private for a decade or more is common now among genuinely strong companies, so it is not automatically a quality signal either way, and it is not irrelevant to risk either: illiquidity duration is real, and an eventual exit, IPO or otherwise, is not guaranteed to preserve or grow the price an unlisted-share investor paid.

body.title: Why the Timeline Stretched
body.textWithBlank: The main reason many strong Indian companies now stay unlisted for a decade or more is the large pool of ___ capital available to them privately.
body.explanation: Late-stage private capital, from growth-equity funds, sovereign wealth funds and large venture funds, now lets companies raise the growth capital an IPO used to be needed for, without ever listing.

cards.definition: A privately held startup valued at $1 billion (roughly ₹8,300 crore) or more in a funding round, without necessarily being listed or profitable.
Large private funding rounds, typically Series C onward, from growth-equity funds, sovereign wealth funds and large venture funds, that let a company raise significant capital without listing.
A funding round that values a company lower than its previous round.

A state-owned investment fund, such as Singapore's GIC and Temasek or the UAE's ADIA and Mubadala, that invests government reserves, including into late-stage private rounds of companies like Indian startups.
A reduction in the value an investor assigns to its existing stake in a private company, made internally on the investor's own books rather than through a new priced round.

points: A flood of late-stage private capital, including from sovereign wealth funds and dedicated growth-equity funds, now lets strong companies raise large rounds without ever listing.
Founders often prefer staying private to avoid public market scrutiny while still scaling, and because secondary sales now solve the liquidity problem an IPO used to solve.
Staying unlisted for a decade or more is increasingly normal and is not, by itself, a sign of either a weak or a strong company.

Every unlisted funding round resets expectations about listing timelines. A company that raised at a certain valuation years ago may be closer to listing, further from it, or quietly marked down since.
An eventual IPO is not automatically a profitable outcome. Public market pricing on listing day, and after, can fall well below the valuation an unlisted-share investor paid to get in.
Before treating a "staying private longer" story as either reassuring or alarming, check for a filed DRHP, recent funding activity, and any reported markdowns.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Vayu Mobility and Meena are fictional and used purely for illustration; the figures shown for Vayu Mobility are illustrative and not real market data. References to Byju's and Paytm describe general, publicly reported events and are included for educational context only, not as a complete or current account of either company. Always verify company-specific facts independently and consult official filings before acting on any unlisted-share opportunity.
